factual_claims.claim: Public benchmarks have shifted from research tools to institutionalized examination and selection devices that influence procurement, investment, and governance decisions.
Exact deduplication of training data does not guarantee the removal of benchmark contamination, as paraphrases, solution fragments, and synthetic variants can still point toward correct answers.
Noisy conditions in benchmark evaluation (deleting, rewriting, and perturbing problems) can systematically outperform clean-control baselines in many LLMs.
As the number of noisy routers increases, the question-level pattern shifts from 'more degraded than improved' to 'more improved than degraded' in LLM benchmark performance.

LLM benchmark scores are influenced by contamination sensitivity, meaning they do not solely reflect model performance on unseen data but also the extent to which test data has leaked into training sets.
Different LLMs exhibit heterogeneous sensitivity to contamination-related cues, meaning similar benchmark scores can have different levels of credibility.
Removing benchmark-related information from LLM training pipelines is challenging due to the scale and heterogeneity of the datasets used.

The use of leaderboard-based competition and promotion in AI development creates incentives for developers to prioritize exam-like benchmark performance, which may inadvertently compromise the model's ability to generalize to real-world tasks.
The router-worker audit framework is designed to detect discrepancies between model performance on novel tasks versus benchmark-specific training data to mitigate score inflation.
In the LLM era, benchmark scores should be viewed as tools requiring careful reinterpretation and auditing rather than as definitive or meaningless metrics.
Benchmark performance should not automatically be read as a direct measure of genuine generalization, because part of what is being captured may reflect sensitivity to contamination-related cues.
